problem: Few RL approaches address audio-only navigation and speaker localization in 3D, and no standard audio RL benchmark exists; prior audio-RL work mostly combines audio with vision or uses simple maze targets.
motivation: Agents that can use auditory cues (alone or with vision) could be more capable, e.g. in games or real-world robots. It is unclear whether an RL agent can localize and identify human speakers from raw stereo audio alone, distinguishing a target speaker from interfering ones, and whether the skill transfers across tasks.
key_idea: Train a small PPO agent (MLP on 2048 raw stereo audio samples) end-to-end in two custom Unity environments, audio-based navigation to a target speaker and microphone-pointing speaker localization, and study generalization and cross-task transfer.
insight: Localizing sources from raw audio is the hard skill in both tasks: fine-tuning from the other task gives faster learning, and zero-shot cross-task evaluation gets 72% SR on navigation (vs 96% trained) and 61% on localization (vs 74%). The 1D CNN gave no gain over the MLP (96% SR both), and the audio buffer length matters (1024 samples best; 4096 hurts, likely by violating the Markov property). Training with 1 utterance per speaker still gave 67% SR on navigation.
method: Agent: PPO with a 2-hidden-layer MLP (256 units each), 2-D continuous output in [-1,1]; input is the latest 1024 samples per stereo channel (about 21 ms at 48 kHz), concatenated into a 2048-vector.

Navigation environment: Unity room with 1-5 stationary speakers at varied heights, one designated target; agent outputs (Vx,Vy); +1 reward for reaching the target, -1 for hitting another speaker or leaving the room, -0.001 per step.

Localization environment: a directional microphone on a gimbal at the room center; agent outputs torques (Tθ,Tφ) for azimuth/elevation; +1 when all 1-5 speakers are pointed at, -0.001 per step, time limit.

Data: about 600 utterances from each of 10 audiobook speakers (VAD segmentation, manually checked). Navigation uses 5 speakers with a 500/100 utterance train/test split; localization uses 5 train and 5 unseen test speakers.
Robustness tests: fewer training utterances (50, 1), reverberation (room, auditorium) and 4-8% pitch shift applied at test time only.
Transfer: pre-train on one task and fine-tune, or evaluate zero-shot on the other. Hyperparameters γ=0.99, c1=0.95, c2=0.001, ε=0.2, 8M training steps.

setting.backbone: PPO with 2-layer MLP (256 units each), trained from scratch; 1D-CNN variant tested
setting.training_data: Online RL in Unity for 8M steps per environment; about 500 audiobook utterances per speaker (5 speakers for navigation; 5 train / 5 test speakers for localization)
setting.observation: raw stereo audio, latest 1024 samples per channel
setting.action_space: continuous 2-D: velocity (Vx,Vy) for navigation; torque (Tθ,Tφ) for microphone azimuth/elevation

results: The PPO agent reaches 96% SR in navigation (human 16%, random 4%) and 74% SR in localization (human 10%, random 2%). It generalizes to unseen utterances and speakers, and is fairly robust to unseen reverberation and pitch shift, with drops of at most 5% SR in navigation and 4% in localization. Cross-task transfer speeds up learning.
limitations: Synthetic Unity environments with simple rooms, stationary speakers and a single agent; no real-world audio or robot, and no standard benchmark comparison.
Weak baselines (random, a single human) and no comparison to other audio-RL or classical localization methods; the 1024-sample buffer is Markov-limited and no memory is used.
Only 100 test episodes per condition, and the localization SR of 74% leaves room for improvement.
